newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ bank bills, futures close on strong note.
newsitem.headline: NZ bank bills, futures close on strong note.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD
OVERNIGHT CASH 9.35 PCT (PREV 9.40) US 5-YR 5.84 (PREV 5.90)
* NZ money market ends bid at Monday's close
* Cullen's comments largely ignored
* December economic and fiscal update fails to inspire
New Zealand's money market coasted to an impressive finish on Monday, with 90-day bank bills and their corresponding futures contract rallying around 16 points.
Dealers said the move came despite an almost static currency and Trade-Weighted Index, although the Kiwi dollar put in a quick show of strength at the close.
The 90-days, which have moved to a March maturity, ended at 8.46 percent.
"The currency and the TWI were pretty much exactly where they were on Friday night, so it's really just been a net rally in the short end," one money market dealer said.
"It was a fantastic day, particularly given that absolutely nothing happened over the weekend."
The gap between the bank bills and futures narrowed substantially. The dealer said the futures were boosted by buying out of Australia at the close, although volumes were not excessive.
"They were just net buyers on the day, but there was nothing big as such," he said.
Dealers said the market had priced in a NZ First-National Party coalition government to emerge from negotiations, which have been taking place since October's inconclusive election.
Labour Party finance spokesperson Michael Cullen caused little stir when he said the high exhange rate would be his first priority if Labour leads the next government.
"He's said that quite a bit before. It's important if Labour gets in, but until we know that it's pretty much irrelevant," one dealer said.

Bonds put in a sizeable rally to end about seven points lower in yield across the curve. Dealers said the 11/06 bond had made sluggish progress but managed to hold in below the crucial 7.00 percent level. It ended at 6.95 percent.
"It's not bad on the face of things, but a pretty poor performance relative to other markets," one dealer said.
He said the market took no notice of Treasury's December economic and fiscal update, which altered forecasts only slightly. Traders were watching to see the shape of the new government, he said.
"People are of the view that the goalposts move at some stage over the next week anyway, so they'll sit and wait for that."
